title: Is there a tool that tells me why my YouTube channel is not growing?
description: Partly. No tool knows for sure, but YouTube Studio shows which stage stalls (reach, click, watch, return) and outside tools check your packaging.
keyword: narrow: Is there a tool that tells me why my YouTube channel is not growing?
body_md:
Partly. No tool can say for certain why a channel is not growing, because the cause sits in one of four places: YouTube is not showing your videos, people see them but do not click, people click but leave early, or viewers never come back. YouTube Studio shows which stage is failing; an outside tool can check your titles and thumbnails.

## Key takeaways

- Growth stalls at one of four stages: reach, click, watch or return.
- YouTube Studio's Reach, Engagement and Audience tabs show which stage is weak, for free.
- Outside tools only see public data, so they help with packaging and upload rhythm, not retention.
- Retention problems need your own retention graph and a rewatch of the drop with sound on.
- Fix the weakest stage first, change one or two things per upload, and measure again.

## The four places growth usually stalls

Think of growth as a funnel. Every view passes through the same four stages:

| Stage | Question | Where to look | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reach | Is YouTube showing your thumbnails? | Reach tab: impressions | Topics viewers want; consistent uploads |
| Click | Do people click when they see them? | Reach tab: impressions click-through rate | Clearer titles and thumbnails |
| Watch | Do they stay once they click? | Engagement tab and audience retention report | Faster openings, tighter structure |
| Return | Do they come back? | Audience tab: new, casual and regular viewers | Series, a steady schedule, a clear channel promise |

On the click stage, YouTube says [half of all channels and videos have an impressions CTR between 2% and 10%](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/7628154). On the return stage, YouTube splits your audience into [new, casual and regular viewers](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/13615784), where regular viewers have returned to watch for at least six months in the past year.

The fix for each stage is different, which is why "why am I not growing?" has no single answer. The first job is to find the stage.

## Step 1: find the weak stage in YouTube Studio (free)

YouTube Studio is the only place with your private numbers. Open **Analytics** from the left menu for the whole channel, or go to **Content**, point to a video and choose **Analytics** ([YouTube Help](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9002587)). Then check:

- **Reach tab:** impressions and impressions CTR. Few impressions points to a reach problem; plenty of impressions with a low CTR points to a packaging problem.
- **Engagement tab:** watch time and average view duration. A steep fall in the first 30 seconds points to a hook problem.
- **Audience tab:** the mix of new, casual and regular viewers. Many new viewers but few returning ones points to a "one-off video" problem.

Write down one number per stage for your last five videos. The stage that is weak across most of them is your bottleneck.

## Step 2: check what a stranger sees

Studio tells you that CTR is low. It does not tell you what is wrong with your titles and thumbnails. An outside view helps here. One option is Asendify's free YouTube Channel Roast on asendify.co: you paste a public channel link, and with no sign-up it scores your titles, thumbnails (from your 8 most recent uploads) and upload consistency, and suggests three fixes. Like any outside tool, it uses public information only. It cannot hear your spoken hook, judge your editing or read your retention graph, so it covers the click stage and part of the return stage, not the others.

You can also do this by hand: line up your last eight thumbnails at phone size and ask whether each one is readable in a second, and whether each title says what the viewer gets.

## Step 3: check the watch stage with your retention data

If Step 1 pointed to retention, open the audience retention report for your weakest recent video. YouTube shows the share of viewers still watching after the first 30 seconds, plus spikes and dips through the video ([YouTube Help](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9314415)). Watch each big drop with the sound on and ask: what made someone leave here?

## Worked example

Example (hypothetical): a cooking channel with 40 videos has had a flat subscriber count for three months. The creator writes down one number per stage for the last five videos.

| Stage | What they found | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Reach | Impressions steady | Fine |
| Click | CTR around 2–3%, the low end of YouTube's typical range | Weak |
| Watch | 30-second retention in line with older videos | Fine |
| Return | Few regular viewers; a three-week upload gap | Weak |

An outside review flags a vague title ("Sunday cooking vlog") and thumbnail text too small for a phone. The diagnosis: the bottleneck is the click stage plus an irregular schedule, not the editing. For the next four uploads, they name the dish and the benefit in each title, use one readable phrase per thumbnail, and keep to a schedule they can sustain. Then they compare CTR and regular viewers. No tool can promise these changes will grow the channel; the value is in knowing which stage to work on first.

## Fixes by stage, in order of effort

Once you know the weak stage, start with the cheapest change.

**Reach**

- Keep uploading on a steady schedule, so YouTube has recent videos to test.
- Choose topics your existing viewers already watch, rather than jumping between niches.
- Look at which past videos brought in new viewers, and make more on that theme.

**Click**

- Rewrite the title of your weakest recent video to name the outcome the viewer gets.
- Simplify the thumbnail to one face or object and a few large words.
- Make sure the title and thumbnail add to each other instead of repeating the same words.

**Watch**

- Remove intros, greetings and sponsor reads from the first 30 seconds.
- Confirm the title's promise within the first few sentences.
- Cut the section at the biggest dip, or add a reason to keep watching just before it.

**Return**

- Group videos into series so one leads naturally to the next.
- End each video by pointing to a specific related video, not a general "subscribe".
- Keep a schedule viewers can rely on.

Change one or two things per upload. If you change everything at once, you will not know what worked.

## What no tool can tell you

- **Whether people want the topic.** If few people care about a subject, better packaging only helps so much. YouTube's Trends tab in Analytics can help you look for ideas viewers are searching for.
- **Why, with certainty.** Numbers show where people stop. You still have to watch the video to see the reason.
- **Results.** Be wary of any tool or service that promises views or subscribers.

## Related guides

Read [where to get a free YouTube channel audit](https://www.asendify.co/blog/where-to-get-free-youtube-channel-audit/), [what retention engineering in YouTube editing is](https://www.asendify.co/blog/what-is-retention-engineering-youtube-editing/) and [the best YouTube video editing agencies](https://www.asendify.co/blog/best-youtube-video-editing-agencies/).

## FAQ

### Is there an AI tool that diagnoses a YouTube channel?

Some AI tools score public packaging, such as titles, thumbnails and upload rhythm. None can see your private analytics without permission, so pair them with YouTube Studio.

### Can an outside tool see my analytics?

Not unless you give it access through Google. Tools that only use public data need no login. For impressions, CTR and retention, use YouTube Studio.

### How many videos do I need before diagnosing growth?

Compare several recent videos rather than judging from one. Five is a sensible minimum for spotting a pattern.

### What if every stage looks fine?

Then look at topic choice and your schedule: are you making videos your audience asks for, and often enough for them to come back?

### What is a good click-through rate?

It depends on the channel and traffic source. YouTube says half of all channels and videos sit between 2% and 10%, so compare against your own past videos first.

title: Where can I get a free YouTube channel audit?
description: Audit your YouTube channel free: YouTube Studio for real retention and traffic data, plus an outside review of titles, thumbnails and upload rhythm.
keyword: narrow: Where can I get a free YouTube channel audit?
body_md:
You can get a free YouTube channel audit from two places: YouTube Studio, which shows your real retention, traffic and click-through data, and free outside tools that review what anyone can see, such as titles, thumbnails and upload rhythm. Use both. The outside view shows what a new viewer sees; YouTube Studio shows what viewers actually did.

## Key takeaways

- A useful audit covers packaging, consistency, retention and direction.
- YouTube Studio is the free, official source for retention and traffic data, and only it has your private numbers.
- Outside tools can only see public data, so they judge packaging and upload rhythm, not what happened after the click.
- Fix one packaging issue and one retention issue per upload, then measure.
- Avoid anyone offering a paid audit who promises views or subscribers.

## What a channel audit should cover

| Question | Area | Where to check | Free? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Do titles and thumbnails make people click? | Packaging | Outside review tools; your own side-by-side comparison | Yes |
| Do you upload often and regularly enough? | Consistency | Your upload history; outside tools | Yes |
| Once people click, do they keep watching? | Retention | YouTube Studio audience retention report | Yes |
| Which videos work, and what next? | Direction | YouTube Studio reach and traffic sources | Yes |

No single free tool covers all four.

## Free option 1: YouTube Studio (your private data)

YouTube Studio is free and is the only place with your real numbers. For an audit, open:

- **The audience retention report** for each recent video. It shows the share of viewers still watching after the first 30 seconds, plus top moments, spikes and dips ([YouTube Help](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9314415)).
- **The typical retention comparison**, which compares a video with your 10 latest videos of similar length.
- **Reach and traffic sources**, to see where viewers find you.

It helps to know what YouTube rewards. YouTube says its recommendations learn from [clicks, watch time, survey responses, shares and likes](https://blog.youtube/inside-youtube/on-youtubes-recommendation-system/). Its discovery advice is to focus on what your audience likes, because ["if you do that and people watch, the recommendations will follow"](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/11914225?hl=en-GB&co=YOUTUBE._YTVideoType%3Dvideo). The [YouTube Creators site](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) has free lessons on reading these reports.

## Free option 2: an outside review of your public packaging

Outside tools look at your channel the way a stranger does. One example is the YouTube Channel Roast, a free tool made by Asendify on asendify.co. You paste your channel link and it reviews your latest public uploads with no sign-up, scoring titles, thumbnails (from your 8 most recent uploads) and upload consistency, and giving three fixes for the week. Like every outside tool, it cannot judge your spoken hook, audio or editing, or read your retention graph, and it needs at least 3 public uploads.

You can also do a manual version: put your last eight thumbnails side by side at phone size, read each title aloud, and ask whether a stranger would know what the video gives them.

## Free option 3: read your own hooks and dips

Outside tools usually miss what happens after the click. Do this part yourself:

- Write out the first 30 seconds of your last three videos. Does each confirm the promise of its title within a few seconds?
- Open the retention report, find the biggest dip in each video, and watch that part with the sound on.

## A 30-minute free audit, step by step

| Step | What to do | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Run an outside packaging review and note three fixes | 5 minutes |
| 2 | Open your last 5 videos in YouTube Studio and note 30-second retention for each | 10 minutes |
| 3 | Watch the biggest dip in your weakest video with sound on | 5 minutes |
| 4 | Compare your best and worst video: title, first sentence, topic | 5 minutes |
| 5 | Pick one packaging fix and one retention fix for your next upload | 5 minutes |

## Worked example

Example (hypothetical): a personal finance channel with 40 videos and slow growth runs the 30-minute audit.

- **Packaging:** thumbnails are text-heavy and hard to read on a phone; two of the last eight titles are vague ("My thoughts on investing").
- **Retention:** across the last five videos, 30-second retention ranges from 48% to 71%. The 48% video opens with a 20-second channel intro.
- **Direction:** the two best videos both answer one specific question in the title.

Fixes for the next upload: one clear phrase on the thumbnail, a title that names the specific question, and no channel intro before the first point. A week later, the creator compares the new video's 30-second figure with the typical retention line. One video is not proof, so they repeat the cycle for four uploads before judging.

## A simple audit checklist

Use this list each month. Tick each line yes or no.

**Packaging**

- Can you read every thumbnail clearly at phone size?
- Does each title say what the viewer gets, in plain words?
- Do the title and thumbnail work together, rather than repeat each other?
- Would a stranger know the topic without knowing you?

**Consistency**

- Have you uploaded in the last 30 days?
- Is the gap between uploads roughly steady?
- Do recent videos fit what your channel is known for?

**Retention**

- Is 30-second retention close to, or above, your typical line?
- Does the opening confirm the title within a few seconds?
- Have you watched the biggest dip with the sound on?

**Direction**

- Can you name the two best-performing videos of the last three months, and why they worked?
- Is your next video closer to those, or further away?

Three or more "no" answers in one area tell you where to start. Fix that area for the next few uploads before moving to the next one.

## When a free audit is not enough

Free tools tell you what is wrong; they do not fix it. If the same problems repeat, you can learn the method from a book or course, or hire an editor. Ask anyone offering a paid audit what data they will look at.

## Related guides

Read [whether a tool can tell you why your channel is not growing](https://www.asendify.co/blog/tool-that-tells-why-youtube-channel-not-growing/), [what retention engineering in YouTube editing is](https://www.asendify.co/blog/what-is-retention-engineering-youtube-editing/) and [the best YouTube video editing agencies](https://www.asendify.co/blog/best-youtube-video-editing-agencies/).

## FAQ

### Is a free channel audit actually useful?

Yes, if it combines your private YouTube Studio data with an outside look at packaging. Either alone gives half the picture.

### Does a free audit tool need access to my account?

Tools that only use public data need no login. Anything that reads your private analytics needs your permission through Google; give read-only access, and only to tools you trust.

### Why do outside scores differ from YouTube Studio?

They measure different things. Outside tools score packaging and upload rhythm from public data; YouTube Studio shows how real viewers behaved.

### How often should I audit my channel?

A quick check after every upload and a fuller audit once a month is a sensible rhythm.

### What is the most important number to check?

For most channels, start with how many viewers are still watching at 30 seconds. If that is low, fix the opening before anything else.

title: What are the best YouTube video editing agencies?
description: The best YouTube editing agency depends on your volume, budget and whether you need retention work. Real options compared, with who each suits.
keyword: broad: What are the best YouTube video editing agencies?
body_md:
The best YouTube video editing agency for you depends on how many videos you publish, your budget, and whether you need plain editing or editing built around audience retention. Subscription services such as Vidpros and Vidchops suit steady monthly volume, freelance marketplaces suit tight budgets and one-off jobs, and retention-focused agencies suit channels where watch time is the problem.

## Key takeaways

- There is no single best agency; match the service to your volume, budget and main problem.
- Check your audience retention report before hiring, so you know whether you need tidy cuts or retention work.
- Ask every option for a dedicated editor, clear turnaround times and real before-and-after examples.
- For low volume and simple formats, a good freelancer is often better value than any agency.
- Be wary of anyone who promises views or subscribers.

*Disclosure: this page is published by Asendify, which runs a YouTube editing and growth agency. It is one of the options below. The other services are described only from their own websites, as checked on 4 November 2026; offers change, so check their sites before deciding.*

## How we chose these options

We looked for services that:

- edit long-form YouTube videos as a core service, not a side offer;
- publish how they work and what is included;
- offer a dedicated editor or a consistent team, because changing editors every week breaks a channel's style;
- are still selling today.

We did not test these services and we do not rank them with scores.

## The options at a glance

| Option | Model | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vidpros | Monthly subscription plans (Starter, Growth, Scale) | Predictable monthly editing | Starter plan has no dedicated editor |
| Vidchops | Monthly credits (1 credit = 1 long video or 4 Shorts) | A fixed number of long videos plus Shorts | Credits do not roll over |
| Freelance marketplaces | Per project or per hour | Small budgets, one-off videos | Quality varies; needs a clear brief |
| Asendify | Retention-focused agency | Channels losing viewers early | Currently full, waitlist only |

## Vidpros: best for a predictable monthly editor

[Vidpros](https://vidpros.com/pricing/) sells editing as monthly subscription plans. As listed on 4 November 2026, its plans are Starter, Growth and Scale, with a dedicated editor on Growth and Scale. Its YouTube page says packages cover assembly, story cut, B-roll, motion graphics, captions, audio mix and colour, with Shorts repurposing, and that it offers white-label work for agencies ([Vidpros](https://vidpros.com/youtube-video-editing-agency/)).

**Choose it if** you upload often and want predictable monthly capacity.

## Vidchops: best for credit-based plans and Shorts

[Vidchops](https://vidchops.com/) runs subscription plans based on monthly credits, where one credit is one long-form video or four short-form videos, and credits do not roll over. Its plans are Vidchops Weekly, Vidchops Pro and Full Time Editor, and it lists a 14-day money-back guarantee.

**Choose it if** you publish a fixed number of long videos a month and want Shorts cut from them.

## Freelance marketplaces: best for small budgets and one-off videos

Marketplaces such as [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/) and [Fiverr](https://www.fiverr.com/) let you hire an individual editor per project or per hour. Quality varies widely, so this route needs more work from you: write a clear brief, ask for a paid test edit, and check samples in your niche.

**Choose it if** you upload occasionally, your format is simple, or you want to try outsourcing before committing to a monthly plan.

## Asendify: best for retention-focused editing (currently waitlist only)

Asendify edits for audience retention: every edit is retention-engineered and made by hand by a dedicated editor, with the same hook, pacing and structure system on every plan. It also edits short-form, podcast, talking-head, finance, gaming, vlog, animation and explainer formats. It is **currently full**, so new clients join a waitlist. If you need an editor this month, one of the other options will suit you better.

**Choose it if** retention is your main problem and you can wait for a place.

## How to choose between them

1. **How many videos a month?** One or two: a freelancer. Four or more: a subscription or agency.
2. **What is the real problem?** If viewers leave in the first 30 seconds, you need retention work, not just tidy cuts. YouTube Studio's [audience retention report](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9314415) shows the share still watching after 30 seconds, and the dips where people leave.
3. **Who edits each week?** Ask whether you get the same editor every time.
4. **How fast are revisions?** Ask for turnaround on first cuts and on revisions.
5. **Can they show results?** Ask for real before-and-after examples.

It also helps to know what YouTube rewards. YouTube says its recommendations learn from [clicks, watch time, survey responses, shares and likes](https://blog.youtube/inside-youtube/on-youtubes-recommendation-system/), so an editor who only makes videos look polished may not fix the problem you have. Read YouTube's own guidance on the [YouTube Creators site](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) so you can brief an editor clearly.

## Worked example: choosing for two channels

Example (hypothetical):

| | Channel A | Channel B |
|---|---|---|
| Uploads | 2 long videos a month | 8 long videos and 20 Shorts a month |
| Retention report | Intro holds well; slow decline after | 40% of viewers leave in the first 30 seconds |
| Main problem | Time to edit | Viewers leaving early |
| Sensible choice | A freelancer with a paid test edit | A retention-focused editor or agency with a dedicated editor |

Channel A does not need an agency; it needs reliable hands. Channel B needs someone who reads the retention graph and changes openings, structure and pacing. The same budget spent on tidy cuts would not fix B's problem.

## Questions to ask any editor or agency

- Will the same editor work on my videos every week?
- Do you ask for my retention graphs before you start?
- What is your turnaround on first cuts and on revisions?
- Can I see a before-and-after retention graph from a real client, with permission?
- What happens if I want to pause or cancel?

Write the answers in one table, so you compare like with like.

## Related guides

Read [what retention engineering in YouTube editing is](https://www.asendify.co/blog/what-is-retention-engineering-youtube-editing/), [where to get a free YouTube channel audit](https://www.asendify.co/blog/where-to-get-free-youtube-channel-audit/) and [whether a tool can tell you why your channel is not growing](https://www.asendify.co/blog/tool-that-tells-why-youtube-channel-not-growing/).

## FAQ

### Is an agency better than a freelance editor?

Not always. A freelancer is often better value for simple formats and low volume. An agency helps when you need steady capacity, cover when an editor is away, or a wider set of skills.

### How much should I budget for YouTube editing?

It ranges from per-video freelance fees to monthly retainers. Volume, length, motion graphics and turnaround speed drive the cost, so get written quotes for your actual format.

### Which agencies focus on audience retention?

Look for ones that ask for your retention graphs before they start and talk about specific drop-off moments. Asendify builds its process around retention, but it is currently waitlist only.

### Can I learn retention editing instead of hiring?

Yes. Start with your own retention reports, fix one leak per upload, and study openings of videos that hold your attention.

### Should I trust an agency that promises more views?

No. Results depend on topic, packaging and audience as well as editing. A good editor promises a process you can check, not numbers.

title: What is retention engineering in YouTube editing and who offers it?
description: Retention engineering means editing a YouTube video around the moments viewers leave, then measuring and repeating. How it works and who offers it.
keyword: narrow: What is retention engineering in YouTube editing and who offers it?
body_md:
Retention engineering is a way of editing YouTube videos where every decision, from the cold open to the cut points and sound, is made to keep viewers watching, then checked against the audience retention graph. The brief becomes "find where people leave and remove the reason". Specialist agencies and some courses offer it, and you can do a basic version yourself.

## Key takeaways

- Retention engineering judges an edit by what viewers do, not how it looks.
- The loop is: read the retention graph, find the dip, change the edit, measure again.
- Start with the first 30 seconds, then structure, pacing, pattern interrupts, captions and sound.
- YouTube Studio's audience retention report is the free, official place to find dips and spikes.
- No honest editor promises views; they offer a process you can check.

## What retention engineering actually means

Most editing is judged by how a video looks. Retention engineering judges an edit by what viewers do. It matters because YouTube says its recommendation system learns from [clicks, watch time, survey responses, shares and likes](https://blog.youtube/inside-youtube/on-youtubes-recommendation-system/), and measures "valued watchtime" through viewer surveys. Holding attention honestly is part of what gets a video recommended.

The working loop:

1. **Read the data.** YouTube Studio's [audience retention report](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9314415) shows the share of viewers still watching after the first 30 seconds, plus top moments, spikes and dips.
2. **Find the leak.** A dip is a section that was skipped or where people stopped watching.
3. **Change the edit.** Tighten, reorder, add a reason to keep watching, or cut the section.
4. **Measure again** on the next upload, and keep what works.

The word "engineering" is there because the process repeats. You treat the video as something you can test and improve.

## The main parts of a retention-engineered edit

| Part | What the editor does | Signal to check |
|---|---|---|
| First 30 seconds | Confirms the title and thumbnail promise fast | Intro retention figure |
| Structure | Open loops, clear payoffs, re-hooks where attention drops | Dips mid-video |
| Pacing and cutting | Removes pauses, repeats and slow set-up; matches pace to energy | Gradual slope of the curve |
| Pattern interrupts | New angle, purposeful B-roll, on-screen text, sound cues | Smaller dips after changes |
| Captions, text, sound | Easy to follow on a phone with low sound | Mobile retention |
| Pre-export checklist | Final pass for common leaks | Fewer repeat problems |

YouTube itself suggests revisiting the title, thumbnail or opening if the intro figure is low. Its discovery guidance adds that if you focus on [what your audience likes and people watch, "the recommendations will follow"](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/11914225?hl=en-GB&co=YOUTUBE._YTVideoType%3Dvideo).

## Worked example

Example (hypothetical): a 12-minute explainer shows a steep fall in the first 30 seconds and a second dip at 4:10.

- **Intro fix.** The original opens with a 25-second channel intro and a "before we start" sponsor mention. The retention edit moves the most surprising claim from 2:00 to the first five seconds, states what the viewer will get, and moves the sponsor read later.
- **Dip at 4:10.** Watching with sound on, the editor finds a long tangent over a static shot. They cut it to two sentences, add a chart as B-roll, and open a loop: "the third reason is the one most people get wrong, and we will get to it".
- **Next upload.** The creator compares the new video's intro figure and dips with "typical retention", which YouTube calculates from your 10 latest videos of similar length.

Suppose the intro figure moves from 55% to 68% on the next video. That is one data point, not proof. Topic, packaging and audience matter too. The point is that each change has a reason you can check, and you keep what keeps working.

## Common leaks and how editors fix them

Most dips come from a small number of causes. When you watch a dip with the sound on, ask which of these it is:

- **A slow start.** Logos, greetings or "before we begin" lines before the promise is confirmed. Fix: open on the most interesting claim or moment, then explain.
- **A broken promise.** The opening does not match the title or thumbnail. Fix: change the opening, or the packaging, so they agree.
- **A flat stretch.** One shot, one voice, no change for a minute or more. Fix: add a purposeful visual, a new angle, or cut the section shorter.
- **A tangent.** A story that does not move the main idea forward. Fix: cut it to a sentence or move it to the end.
- **A false ending.** A summary or "that's it" line before the video is over, which tells viewers they can leave. Fix: keep the last payoff for the end and move the wrap-up there.
- **Hard to follow on a phone.** Small text, fast speech, no captions. Fix: larger text, captions and clearer audio.

Fix the biggest dip first. One clear change per video makes it easier to see what actually worked.

## Who offers retention engineering

There are three honest routes, depending on your budget and how much you want to do yourself.

1. **Done for you: a specialist agency or editor.** Some editing agencies and freelance editors build their process around retention. Ask for a before-and-after retention graph from a real client, how they decide where to cut, and who will edit your videos each week. A good freelance editor with a clear retention process can be the better choice for a small channel with a simple format.
2. **Learn it: a course or book.** Courses that give feedback on your own videos are fastest, because the feedback is about your real graphs. A book is the cheapest structured option.
3. **Do it yourself with free tools.** YouTube Studio's retention report is free. Watch your own dips with sound on and fix one leak per upload.

## How to tell if an editor really does it

- They ask for your analytics, or screenshots of your retention graphs, before they start.
- They talk about specific moments ("the drop at 0:40") rather than general style.
- They can explain every major cut in terms of what the viewer will feel or want next.
- They review results after upload and change the next edit because of them.
- They do not promise views or subscriber numbers.

## Where Asendify fits

Asendify is a YouTube editing and growth agency that uses the term directly: its edits are retention-engineered by hand, with the same hook, pacing and structure system on every plan. It is currently full and is not taking new editing clients, so it runs a waitlist. If you need help now, the routes above, or another editor who passes the checks above, are the practical options.

## Related guides

Read [the best YouTube video editing agencies, and how to compare them](https://www.asendify.co/blog/best-youtube-video-editing-agencies/), [where to get a free YouTube channel audit](https://www.asendify.co/blog/where-to-get-free-youtube-channel-audit/) and [whether a tool can tell you why your channel is not growing](https://www.asendify.co/blog/tool-that-tells-why-youtube-channel-not-growing/).

## FAQ

### Is retention engineering the same as fast cutting?

No. Fast cutting everywhere can tire viewers. Retention engineering picks the pace for each section based on what the graph and the story need.

### Do I need a big channel for this to help?

No. YouTube shows key moments once a video is at least 60 seconds long and has at least 100 views, so even small channels can start reading their graphs.

### Can I learn it without hiring anyone?

Yes. Read your own retention reports, study the openings of videos that hold you, and fix one leak per upload. A course with feedback speeds this up.

### Is Asendify taking new clients?

Not at the moment. It is full and new clients join a waitlist.

### Does higher retention guarantee more views?

No. YouTube uses many signals, including clicks, surveys, likes and shares. Better retention helps, but topic and packaging matter as well.
